question: More than 20 years after the EU’s largest enlargement, all six sites of the Joint Research Centre (JRC) are still located in five countries of the ‘old’ Union: Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain. None of the 13 countries that joined the EU in 2004 or later hosts a JRC centre, although they all co-fund its laboratories, infrastructure and jobs.

In its resolution of 25 October 2018 on the relocation of the European Medicines Agency (EMA), Parliament criticised the widening geographical imbalance in the distribution of EU agencies, pointing out that only 9 of the 37 decentralised agencies were located in the new Member States.

Poland – the largest country in the region, with significant scientific potential, an extensive research base and a skilled workforce – is a natural candidate for hosting the JRC’s research activities. 1.
What objective grounds does the Commission cite to justify the concentration of all JRC sites exclusively in countries that joined the EU before 2004?

Does the Commission regard this concentration as an imbalance similar to that highlighted by Parliament with regard to the decentralised agencies, and if not, on what grounds does it justify a different approach in respect of the JRC?
In the event of any future reorganisation, relocation or redistribution of the JRC’s activities, will the Commission consider locating a research centre in Poland?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.11.2026) The Joint Research Centre (JRC) was created under the Euratom Treaty of 1957 to coordinate nuclear research and avoid duplication of national programmes.

Unlike seats of decentralised Union Agencies, whose host cities are chosen through competitive site-selection, JRC sites were established by taking over national installations (Ispra, Petten) and setting up Community laboratories next to national centres (Geel, Karlsruhe). Its nuclear sites are subject to strict legal obligations including licensing by the host Member State, and decommissioning of legacy facilities.

Relocating a nuclear site would require new host-state licences and considerable budgetary resources. More importantly, no EU institution has identified any need for such a move. Any potential relocation of a JRC site would be difficult and costly, given the nuclear nature of four of the sites and the level of investment in the scientific infrastructures.

It would therefore require thorough justification and reasoning. Relocating a JRC (nuclear) site cannot be compared with designating the seat of a newly established decentralised agency which consists only of offices for its staff. The Commission is currently not aware of any call or need to relocate any of the JRC sites.

Poland, as all the Members States, is involved in several ways in JRC’s work and activities: it is represented on the JRC’s Board of Governors, and the JRC cooperates with relevant Polish research organisations through its network of collaboration agreements1.

Finally, the research run by the JRC serves the common EU interest and policymaking well beyond Horizon Europe2 and Euratom3 programmes, supporting a wide range of EU policies and all Member States benefit through those JRC direct actions.
1 JRC collaborates with Państwowa Agencja Atomistyki in the area of nuclear safeguards (ESARDA) and via
network for the exchange of radiological monitoring data (EURDEP). JRC collaborates with Uniwersytet Jagielloński (UJ) on Large Enriched Germanium Experiment for Neutrinoless Decay (LEGEND).

JRC also signed bilateral instruments like: Collaboration Agreement and Collaborative Doctoral Partnership with Narodowe Centrum Badań Jądrowych (NCBJ); Memorandum of Understanding with Sieć Badawcza Łukasiewicz Collaboration Agreement with Politechnika Krakowska; Collaboration Agreement with Instytut Ochrony Środowiska – Państwowy Instytut Badawczy (IOŚ-PIB). 2 https://research-and-innovation.ec.europa.
